Anila Mobility: The Gap Between Booking and Delivery

Forty-one thousand eight hundred people paid Anila Mobility a token this festive season. Twelve thousand nine hundred took delivery. Six explanations fit the evidence; three of them contradict each other; and the board meets on Tuesday.

1. Sunday night, Baner

At twenty past eleven on the night of Sunday, 22 November 2026, Aniruddh Barve was still at the dining table of his flat in Baner, Pune, with a laptop, a printed board pre-read, and a cup of tea that had gone cold an hour earlier. Ani, as everyone at Anila Mobility called him, was the company's Vice-President of Digital Product. He had joined in 2023 from a payments company in Bengaluru, largely because Anila's founder had described the job as "making buying a scooter feel like buying a phone".

The pre-read on the table had been circulated by the office of the chief financial officer four days earlier. On page six was a chart with a single highlighted row: token-to-invoice conversion, 58.4% (Aug) → 31.1% (Oct). The board's agenda item, scheduled for 11:15 on Tuesday, was titled "Festive funnel: diagnosis and remediation plan", and Rukmini Deshmukh, the chief executive, had asked Ani to send her a one-page recommendation by nine o'clock on Monday morning so that she could read it on her flight from Pune to Mumbai.

Ani had spent the weekend assembling every number he could find, and the exercise had made him less certain rather than more. He had six documents in front of him. At least two of them could not both be true.

2. How Anila got here, and the decision that still binds it

Anila Mobility was founded in 2019 by Rukmini Deshmukh, a former powertrain engineer, and two colleagues from her time at an auto-components supplier in Chakan. Its first vehicle, the Anila Surya, a 2.9 kWh electric scooter with a claimed 108 km range, reached customers in late 2021 at ₹1.09 lakh ex-showroom. By 2026 the company sold two models — the Surya at ₹1.24 lakh and the Surya X, launched in June 2026, at ₹1.42 lakh — and had delivered a little over 1.4 lakh vehicles in total. It employed 1,180 people, manufactured at a plant near Chakan, and had raised ₹1,240 crore across three rounds.

The decision that shaped everything Ani could and could not do had been taken in March 2022. Facing the choice between building a conventional dealer network and following the "digital-first, dealer-light" model that several Indian electric two-wheeler companies had adopted, Anila chose the latter: customers would configure and book online, pay a ₹2,000 refundable token, and complete the purchase at one of the company's experience centres. To run the back end, Anila licensed a dealer-management system from Trikon Systems, a Chennai vendor, on a six-year contract running to March 2028. The customer-facing website, configurator and checkout were built in-house on a different stack.

The two systems were never joined. Trikon's DMS identified customers by a dealer-order number; Anila's web stack identified them by an anonymous device identifier and, after login, a mobile number that was hashed before it left the app under the company's reading of its obligations following the DPDP Act. A proposal in early 2023 to introduce a common customer key had been costed at ₹2.4 crore and deferred. The consequence, four years later, was simple and total: Anila could measure everything that happened before the token was paid, and everything that happened after, and it could not connect the two for any individual customer.

The dealer-light model itself had been quietly abandoned in 2024, when growth stalled and the company signed 120 franchise partners across tier-2 and tier-3 India to sit alongside its 40 company-owned experience centres. Franchise partners were paid a fee on every booking they originated and a smaller margin on every delivery. Nobody had revisited that ratio since.

3. The industry around it

India's electric two-wheeler market in 2026 was competitive in a way that left very little room for a mid-sized independent. Ola Electric, Ather Energy, TVS with the iQube, Bajaj with the Chetak and Hero MotoCorp with Vida between them took the large majority of monthly registrations recorded on the VAHAN portal, and all of them could sustain discounting that Anila could not. Ather in particular had built a reputation among the same urban, engineering-literate buyers Anila targeted.

Two forces from outside the industry bore directly on the festive quarter. The first was subsidy. Central support for electric two-wheelers under the PM E-DRIVE scheme was structured to step down, and the per-vehicle incentive available in the second half of the financial year was lower than it had been in the first. Anila's marketing had chosen not to feature the subsidy prominently, on the grounds that the amount was confusing to explain; Anila's call centre reported that customers asked about it constantly.

The second was credit. Nearly four-fifths of Anila's customers financed the purchase, mostly through two non-banking financial companies with whom Anila had origination arrangements, referred to internally as NBFC-1 and NBFC-2. Retail credit conditions had tightened through 2026, and lenders across the Indian consumer-durables and two-wheeler segments had grown more selective about thin-file and first-time borrowers — precisely the customers a festive campaign in tier-3 India brings in.

Anila also had an export thread. Nadeen Fleet Services, a Dubai last-mile logistics operator, had issued a letter of intent for 2,400 units for its delivery riders, contingent on Gulf homologation, a 60V charging variant and firm delivery dates beginning March 2027. At roughly ₹1.06 lakh a unit landed, the order was worth about ₹25 crore and would absorb a meaningful share of the company's unsold inventory.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The festive campaign launched on 1 September with a budget of ₹22 crore, the largest marketing commitment in the company's history, negotiated by Rukmini with the board on the argument that Anila needed to establish scale before its Series D. September went well: bookings rose 2.1 times over August, and October's numbers, when they arrived, looked extraordinary. Bookings for the two months together reached 41,800 against a plan of 24,000.

Three things were believed inside the company in mid-October. First, that the campaign was working. Second, that deliveries would follow bookings with the usual four-to-six week lag. Third, that the funnel was healthy, because the web analytics dashboard — which the growth team reviewed weekly and the product team owned — showed conversion at every measured step holding steady or improving.

By mid-November all three beliefs were in some difficulty. Deliveries had risen, but nothing like proportionately. Against 41,800 bookings in September and October, 12,900 vehicles had been invoiced by 15 November. The CFO's team computed token-to-invoice conversion at 31.1 percent for the October cohort against 58.4 percent for August, and it was this single comparison that had become the centre of gravity of the board pre-read.

Since the pre-read was circulated, three facts had come to light, each of which unsettled the comparison.

On 3 October, the marketing team had reduced the token from ₹2,000 to ₹499 as a "festive offer", a change made in a campaign brief and never reviewed by product or finance. Ani discovered this on 19 November. The DMS records both amounts under a single status, token received; the distinction exists only in the payment gateway export, which is a separate file, and which does not carry the dealer-order number. An approximate reconciliation by transaction amount and timestamp suggested that roughly 61 percent of October bookings were ₹499 bookings, but the match rate was imperfect and the analytics team would not stand behind the figure.

On 14 October, NBFC-2 had tightened its credit policy for first-time borrowers, raising its minimum bureau score and adding an income-document requirement. The notification was an email to Anila's finance operations team; it was forwarded to the retail network team on 6 November and reached Ani on 17 November. NBFC-2 handled 46 percent of Anila's financed volume.

On 12 October, the call centre's customer relationship platform had been upgraded, and the agent disposition dropdown had been reordered and two codes added. Nobody had recorded what the previous ordering was.

5. The people

Rukmini Deshmukh, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Her stated position is that this is a product and experience problem: forty-one thousand people wanted an Anila, and the company failed to convert them, which is a failure of the buying journey. Her incentive is the Series D, for which a term sheet is in negotiation and in which booking growth is the headline number in the deck. What she has not said to the team is that the lead investor's diligence request, received on 10 November, asks specifically for token-to-delivery conversion by month for the last eight quarters.

Sridhar Venkatesan, Vice-President of Engineering, Bengaluru. His position is that no honest answer is possible until the web stack and the DMS share a customer key, and he has costed the re-platform at ₹6.2 crore over nine months. His incentive is a hard one to discuss: his platform team has lost four engineers in six months and he believes a large, visible project is the only way to keep the rest. He has not said that the Trikon contract carries a ₹4.1 crore early-termination charge if Anila migrates before March 2028, a clause he learned about a fortnight ago.

Neelam Krishnan, lead data scientist, Toronto. Her position, stated in an internal memo on 16 November, is that none of the existing exhibits can distinguish between four competing explanations and that the company should run a holdout rather than argue. Her incentive is professional: she raised the customer-key problem in 2023 and was overruled, and the present situation vindicates her. She has not said that a holdout of the size she wants would take until February to read out, which is well past the board's patience.

Katharina Vogel, design lead, Berlin. Her position is that the configurator is the problem: it asks buyers to choose between two models, four colours, three battery-warranty options and an accessories bundle, and her review of 46 session recordings shows a median of eleven minutes and a high rate of back-navigation. Her incentive is a visible win; she has an offer from a Munich firm that she has not mentioned and has told a colleague she wants to "finish something real" before deciding.

Meghna Pillai, Head of Retail Network, Pune and travelling. Her position is that the funnel is fine and the problem is downstream: delivery timelines on the Surya X stretched to nine weeks in October, and customers who had paid a token were cancelling because they could get an Ather or a TVS the same week. Her incentive is the network she built; the franchise partners are hers. She has not volunteered that franchise partners earn ₹1,100 on a booking and ₹1,900 on a delivery, so that a partner facing a slow month has every reason to generate tokens whether or not the customer is likely to buy.

Sanjay Rathi, chief financial officer, Pune. His position is the balance sheet: ₹8.36 crore of refundable token money sits as a liability, 9,100 finished units sit in inventory at roughly ₹96 crore of cost, and the festive quarter will miss its revenue plan by about ₹38 crore. He wants the ₹499 token withdrawn immediately. He has not said that his own team's monthly reporting pack had shown the token-to-invoice number falling since early October and that the decline was described in the pack's commentary as "seasonal mix".

Arvind "Andy" Sundaram, Head of International Business, New Jersey. His position is that the Dubai order should be accelerated: 2,400 units absorbs a quarter of the inventory overhang at a healthy margin and is not exposed to Indian retail credit at all. His incentive is that his variable compensation is weighted to export bookings. He has not said that Nadeen's letter of intent contains a clause allowing withdrawal without penalty if homologation is not complete by 15 February.

Faisal Rehman, general manager, Nadeen Fleet Services, Dubai. His position, conveyed on a call at 2 p.m. Gulf time on 19 November, is that he needs a firm commitment before 15 December to include the vehicles in his 2027 operating plan. What he has not said to Andy is that he has taken a meeting with another manufacturer and is comparing total cost of ownership over four years, not purchase price.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Lay Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 side by side. What, precisely, does each one measure, and what would have to be true for both of them to be accurate descriptions of the same festive quarter?

2. The board pre-read's headline comparison is 58.4 percent against 31.1 percent. Using Exhibit 6, restate that comparison in a way you would be willing to defend. How much of the apparent collapse survives your restatement, and how much of the remainder can you attribute with confidence?

3. Exhibit 3 says 5.6 percent of contacted customers cite declined finance; Exhibit 5 implies that finance declines rose sharply. Exhibit 4 says franchise partners convert test rides better than company centres. For each of these three exhibits, identify how it was produced and what that production process does to what it can be used to conclude.

4. The token changed from ₹2,000 to ₹499 on 3 October. Trace the consequences of that single change through every exhibit in this case. Which comparisons in the board pre-read remain valid afterwards?

5. Four explanations are live: a lender's credit policy, a change in the composition of bookings, delivery timelines, and the design of the buying journey. For each, state the cheapest piece of evidence that would raise or lower your confidence in it, and say whether Anila can obtain that evidence before 1 December. What does your answer imply about Sridhar's re-platform proposal?

6. It is 6 a.m. on Monday. What does Ani send Rukmini at nine o'clock, and what does he ask the board for on Tuesday? If the board asks him the direct question — "so which step is leaking?" — what is his honest answer, and how does he say it without either overclaiming or appearing to have nothing?

11. Sunday, 11:50 p.m.

Ani had arranged the six exhibits across the dining table like a hand of cards. His phone showed a message from Neelam in Toronto, sent at her lunchtime: "Whatever you write, please don't put a single conversion number on the first line." Below it was one from Andy in New Jersey, sent forty minutes later: "Faisal is asking again. 15 Dec is real." Below that, nothing from Rukmini, who had said everything she intended to say on Tuesday of the previous week.

He thought about the boy in Nashik in Meghna's voice note, and about the 1,421 customers who had given no reason because the dropdown's first entry was no reason, and about the ₹2.4 crore that had not been spent in February 2023 and the ₹6.2 crore it would now cost. He thought about the fact that somewhere inside the 24,500 October tokens were several thousand people who still wanted a scooter and were waiting for a call that nobody was going to make this week because the company was busy arguing about which step had leaked.

The page in front of him had a heading, Recommendation, and beneath it three bullet points he had written and rewritten four times. At ten minutes to midnight he deleted all three, wrote a single sentence at the top of the page, read it back, and could not decide whether it was the most honest thing he had written all month or a sentence that would end his career at Anila Mobility.

Reading Drop-off: Which Step Leaks, and What the Numbers Won't Tell You

On the second Tuesday of August 2026, Ananya Rao, senior product analyst at Paidan Health, opened the funnel dashboard she had built eighteen months earlier and found the number that would define her week: 40 percent. That was the share of users who viewed the details of a diagnostic test package on the Paidan app and did not add it to their cart. Paidan, a Bengaluru-based platform that lets households book blood tests and imaging scans from NABL-accredited labs for home collection, had just closed a fresh funding round on the strength of a growth story, and its VP of Growth, Vikram Oswal, wanted to spend a third of the new marketing budget driving more traffic into the top of exactly this funnel. Founder and CEO Meenal Kapoor had one question for Ananya before she would sign off: if the funnel already leaks 40 percent at the cart step, why would we pay to fill it faster? Ananya had built the funnel chart many times before. What she had not yet done, carefully, was read it — separate what the drop-off number could tell her from what it could only make her guess at. Get this wrong and Paidan would spend roughly nine lakh rupees a month acquiring users who were mathematically certain to hit the same wall partway through the very journey the money was meant to complete.

The Idea

A funnel takes a multi-step journey — app open, search, view a product, add to cart, pay — and counts, at each step, how many of the people who reached the previous step made it to this one. Drop-off is simply what is left over: the users counted at one step who are not counted at the next. The idea has two intertwined ancestors. In 1898, the advertising theorist Elias St. Elmo Lewis proposed that a buyer moves through stages of Attention, Interest, Desire and Action — the first funnel, drawn to explain why an advertisement's audience shrinks before anyone buys. A century later, as web and mobile products generated event-level data at a scale no salesperson's notebook ever could, analytics practitioners such as Avinash Kaushik popularized applying the same shrinking-stages logic to a single digital session, and platforms built in the early 2010s — Mixpanel, Amplitude, and their peers — turned it into a chart every product team could generate in minutes. What Ananya needed to be able to say to Meenal Kapoor, without sounding glib, was this: a funnel tells you exactly where in a journey people stop, but it can never tell you why they stopped — that second answer has to come from somewhere else.

How It Actually Works

Reading a funnel well requires more discipline than building one. The mechanical part — set an order of events, count distinct users reaching each in sequence, divide each step's count by the one before it — is the part every analytics tool now does automatically, and it is the part most practitioners stop at. What separates someone who merely runs a funnel report from someone who understands drop-off is what happens after the percentages appear. First, a careful reader distinguishes the step conversion rate (this step's users divided by the prior step's users) from the absolute number lost, because a small percentage drop against a huge population and a large percentage drop against a small one can cost the business the same number of customers. Second, a careful reader interrogates the event definitions themselves — what exactly counts as "viewed a test," a single page render or a minimum dwell time — because a drop-off figure inherits every ambiguity baked into how the underlying events were logged. Third, a careful reader checks whether the population entering the funnel this period is the same kind of population that entered it last period, since a funnel compares stages of one journey, not stages across different journeys taken by different people. Only once those three checks are done does the number mean what it appears to mean — the step where the business, not just the metric, is actually losing money.

Fig. 1 — Width of each bar is proportional to users remaining; the step-4 bar (view to cart, 40%) is the steepest single drop by percentage, but not necessarily the costliest in absolute users lost.

A Worked Example

Table 1 lays out July's numbers the way Ananya first saw them. Reading only the "step conversion" column, the eye jumps immediately to step 4 — view to cart — at 40 percent, the lowest rate in the chain, and it is tempting to declare that the cart step is "the" leak. But the absolute-drop column tells a closer story: step 2 (search to view) loses 17,500 users at a comfortable-looking 75 percent conversion, and step 4 loses 31,500 at 40 percent — nearly double, and clearly the largest single loss of people anywhere in the journey. On a base of 100,000 monthly sessions, at an average order value of ₹850, the 11,025 completed bookings generate roughly ₹93.7 lakh a month. If Ananya could lift the cart-step conversion rate from 40 to 55 percent — holding the 52,500 test-viewers constant — the arithmetic runs: 52,500 × 0.55 = 28,875 carts, × 0.75 = 21,656 address completions, × 0.70 = 15,159 payments, generating ₹1.288 crore a month, a gain of roughly ₹35 lakh from fixing one step, without spending a rupee on acquisition.

Every downstream rate stays fixed at July's levels, so: 130,000 × 0.70 = 91,000 searches; × 0.75 = 68,250 views; × 0.40 = 27,300 carts. The absolute number of people lost at the cart step alone rises from 31,500 to 40,950 — nearly 9,500 more people, each one acquired at real cost, hitting precisely the same wall. Carrying the rest through: 27,300 × 0.75 = 20,475 addresses, × 0.70 = 14,332 payments. Overall conversion is 14,332 / 130,000 = 11.0 percent — statistically identical to July. The spend does not move the rate at all; it only makes the pipe leak more people, in absolute terms, at exactly the point that was already broken. That single recomputation is the whole answer to the CEO's question, expressed as arithmetic rather than opinion.

The Nuances

Percentage versus absolute loss. A step's conversion rate and the number of people it costs the business are different questions, and prioritizing by the scarier-looking percentage, rather than by the largest absolute loss (or the loss multiplied by its value), routinely sends teams to fix the wrong step.

Definitions decide the answer. Whether "viewed a test" means a page load, a three-second dwell, or a scroll past the price, changes every downstream percentage; two analysts can log the same product differently and produce two defensibly different funnels from the same user behavior.

Drop-off blends intenders and browsers. The users counted as "lost" at a step include people who tried and failed alongside people who never meant to continue — a price-comparer checking Paidan against Tata 1mg was never going to buy this session — and the funnel has no way to separate the two populations.

Time windows can manufacture leaks. A booking journey that naturally spans two days will show enormous drop-off in a funnel measured over a single session window, not because anyone abandoned, but because the analyst's clock ran out before the user's did.

Mixed cohorts hide the real leak. Combining first-time and repeat users, or app and mobile-web traffic, into one funnel can average away a severe leak in one segment against a healthy rate in another, so the aggregate number looks unremarkable while a real problem sits underneath it.

A rate is where, never why. The funnel can say with confidence that 31,500 people stopped between viewing and adding to cart; it cannot say whether they were deterred by price, by a slow page, or by a payment method they distrust — that requires session recordings, exit surveys, or usability sessions, and a guessed cause is often the wrong one.

Comparisons need a constant population. A conversion rate that falls from one month to the next may reflect a genuine product regression, or it may simply reflect that the acquisition channel mix shifted toward lower-intent traffic; the two explanations require completely different responses, and the raw funnel cannot distinguish them without being re-cut by channel.

Consumer, B2B, and Marketplace

Paidan's funnel is short and high-volume, resolving within a single sitting, which is typical of consumer products: drop-off can be read at a daily cadence because the sample size is large and the journey is fast. A B2B software company such as Utaar Systems, selling compliance workflow tools to mid-sized manufacturers, faces a funnel spanning weeks — trial signup, workspace configuration, inviting teammates, first paid seat — where each step can involve a human procurement decision invisible to the product, and where small monthly cohorts make week-to-week percentage swings mostly noise rather than signal; Utaar's analysts read funnels as slow-moving cohort curves, not daily dashboards. A marketplace like Zeena Mart, connecting kirana stores with wholesale suppliers, runs two funnels at once, buyer and seller, and a leak on the supply side changes what buyers see and therefore reshapes the buyer-side funnel too, so the two must be read together rather than optimized in isolation. Stage matters as much as business model: an early-stage company with a few thousand monthly sessions should treat a step's percentage move with real suspicion until it persists across several weeks, while a company at Paidan's scale can trust a one-point shift in the cart-step rate as real money, worth an engineering sprint to chase.

Common Mistakes

Chasing the reddest percentage. Symptom: a team fixates on the step with the lowest conversion rate on the dashboard, regardless of how many people that step actually costs. Underlying error: mistaking a ratio for a magnitude. Cheapest diagnostic: before any step is prioritized, sort all steps by absolute users lost, not by percentage, and only then bring the percentages back in as a second cut.

Pouring water into a leaking pipe. Symptom: acquisition spend rises, top-of-funnel volume rises, but the overall conversion percentage does not move, quarter after quarter. Underlying error: treating a top-of-funnel and a mid-funnel problem as the same lever. Cheapest diagnostic: before increasing spend, hold the weakest step's own conversion rate up against last quarter's — if it hasn't moved, more traffic will not move it either.

Turning a location into a cause. Symptom: a product note reads "60 percent drop at the cart page means users don't trust our payment options," with no evidence offered beyond the number itself. Underlying error: treating drop-off as an answer rather than a question. Cheapest diagnostic: watch a genuinely small sample — fifteen or twenty session recordings of exactly that step — before writing a causal sentence about it.

Comparing apples across a channel shift. Symptom: a redesign is declared a failure because the funnel's overall rate fell the week after launch. Underlying error: not checking whether the traffic mix changed at the same time. Cheapest diagnostic: rerun the same funnel filtered to a single, unchanged acquisition channel before attributing any rate change to the redesign.

What Good Looks Like

Ananya does not walk into Meenal Kapoor's office with the 40 percent figure. She walks in having sorted every step by absolute users lost, having confirmed the event definitions for "view" and "cart" had not silently changed between app releases, and having watched fifteen session recordings of users who viewed a test and left without adding it to cart. In twelve of the fifteen, the pattern is the same: the discounted package price is not shown until the user opens the cart drawer, and the individually listed component-test prices on the detail page sum to a number nearly 30 percent higher, producing a moment that looks, on video, exactly like sticker shock. She proposes showing the bundled price on the detail page itself, a two-week engineering change, and separately recommends Vikram hold the acquisition increase for three weeks so any rate change can be measured against a stable population.

Closing

Meenal Kapoor approves the price-transparency fix and pauses the spend increase pending the re-measurement Ananya proposed. The reasoning she gives the board is not "our funnel showed a leak" — every funnel shows a leak somewhere — but that the leak's size in absolute users, its likely cause confirmed by direct observation, and the arithmetic showing marketing spend would not touch the underlying rate, together made the fix the only defensible next move. Ananya's next stop, appropriately, is friction audits and step counting: now that she knows where the leak sits, she needs a disciplined way to enumerate the individual frictions inside that one step and weigh them against each other, rather than relying on which twelve session recordings happened to be vivid. Two questions worth sitting with: the last time a drop-off percentage alarmed you, did you ask how many actual people that number represented, or only how sharp the ratio looked? And could you say, with evidence rather than assumption, that the users entering your funnel this month are drawn from the same population as the users who entered it the month you are comparing against?

Reading Drop-off: The Step That Leaks, the Sieve That Works, and the Difference Between Them

Every funnel leaks somewhere. The analytical work is deciding which leak is a defect, which is the product doing its job, which is an artefact of how the measurement was built, and which of them would actually pay for the engineering it would take to fix.

1. Two Rooms, Two Numbers

At 7:40 on the morning of 3 September 2026, in a converted bungalow off Baner Road in Pune, Malini Bhatt pulled up the August application funnel for Nithaar Money and looked for the third day running at the number 62. Nithaar was a four-year-old digital lending app: small-ticket personal loans, average principal ₹68,000, originated through a partner NBFC, with a savings product attached. Of the 34,320 people who had accepted a loan offer in August, only 62 percent — 21,278 — had completed the income-verification step that followed it. Thirteen thousand and forty-two people had looked at an offer they liked, tapped through, been asked to share six months of bank statements, and vanished.

Malini's head of growth wanted the step deleted, or at minimum replaced by an Account Aggregator flow that pulled the statements in one consent tap. The credit head, Farhan Qureshi, dialling in from the risk team's floor in Mumbai, wanted it left exactly where it was. The board met on 24 September. Malini had three weeks to decide what the 62 actually meant, and her difficulty was not that she lacked data. It was that four different, internally coherent stories — friction, price rejection, deliberate credit screening, and a logging defect in the Android release shipped on 11 August — all produced a number close to 62.

Eighteen hundred kilometres north, in Gurugram, Devang Puri had the opposite problem: a number so bad that everyone in the room had already agreed on its meaning. Chhalni Systems sold quality-inspection software to FMCG and pharmaceutical manufacturers — a tablet app for line inspectors, a dashboard for quality heads, and connectors into the customer's warehouse-management and ERP systems. Devang ran the self-serve business unit, which had been launched to short-circuit an eleven-month enterprise sales cycle. Of the 340 trials that started in the second quarter of 2026, 255 got as far as creating a workspace, and only 74 ever connected a single data source. Seventy-one percent of trials died at the connector.

On 28 August, Devang's engineering lead, Sujata Menon, read the same cohort report and said something that stopped the meeting: most of those aren't dead, they're slow. The quarter's funnel had been measured ninety days after trial start. In enterprise manufacturing, she argued, ninety days did not cover a customer's own IT security review. If she was right, Devang's plan — six of his forty engineers for a quarter, rebuilding the connector framework — would be solving a problem that mostly did not exist. If she was wrong, and he waited, the self-serve unit would miss its second annual target and be folded back into field sales.

2. The Idea, and Who Disagrees About It

Define the object precisely, because most arguments about drop-off are arguments about definitions conducted as if they were arguments about the world. A funnel is an ordered list of events e1, e2, … eK, a population of entities (users, accounts, sessions, devices) that performed e1 within some entry window, and a conversion window W inside which each subsequent event must occur for the entity to be counted at that step. The step conversion rate rk is the count at step k divided by the count at step k−1. Drop-off at step k is 1 − rk, which statisticians would recognise as a discrete-time hazard: the probability of failing at k conditional on having survived to k−1. Overall conversion is the product ∏rk, which is why funnels punish length so brutally.

Three choices are hidden inside that definition and they are where practitioners quietly differ. Strictness: must ek follow ek−1 with no other events in between (strict), or merely after it (loose)? Grain: is the entity a session, a user, or an account — and if a user tries three times in a week, is that one entity or three? Window: how long may an entity take, and what happens to entities that entered too recently to have finished? Two competent analysts handed the same event stream and told to build "the checkout funnel" will produce different numbers, and both will be right, because they answered those three questions differently.

The intellectual history has four distinct tributaries, and knowing which one a colleague is drinking from explains most disagreements. The sales-pipeline line runs from Elias St. Elmo Lewis's 1898 stage model through William W. Townsend's 1924 rendering of it as an actual funnel shape: its instinct is that stages are real, sequential, and that the job is to widen the narrow ones. The industrial-yield line runs from statistical process control into Six Sigma's rolled throughput yield, and its instinct is opposite: that a multi-stage process loses most of its output to the accumulation of many small, unremarkable losses, and that the highest-leverage move is usually to remove a stage, not improve one. The survival-analysis line, from actuarial life tables through Kaplan and Meier's 1958 estimator, brings the vocabulary of hazard, censoring and competing risks, and its instinct is that discretising a continuous process into steps throws away the information that matters. The web-analytics line — log-file path analysis in the late 1990s, Google Analytics' goal funnels from 2005, then the event-model tools of the early 2010s — contributed the thing that made drop-off ubiquitous: a chart any product manager could generate in ninety seconds without asking an analyst, and therefore without being asked the three questions above.

The problem the funnel was invented to solve is worth stating plainly, because it is easy to lose: before the funnel, a firm losing customers knew only that it was losing them. The funnel's contribution is localisation. It converts an undifferentiated loss into a coordinate. What it conspicuously does not do — and what four schools of thought have spent a century failing to agree about — is tell you whether the coordinate marks a wound or a valve.

3. Mechanics in Depth

The first thing an expert notices in Table 2 is not the 62. It is that the step rates rise as you go down. This is almost always true, in almost every funnel, and it is very rarely a fact about the product. Suppose each entrant i carries a latent propensity pi to complete the whole journey. Surviving a step is evidence of high pi, so the population at step k is a sample of the entry population re-weighted toward high propensity: formally, E[p | survived to k] is non-decreasing in k. Later steps therefore face easier customers and post better rates even if they are worse designed. Comparing step 8's 95 percent against step 5's 62 percent as though they were competing pieces of craftsmanship is comparing a test written for a self-selected group of finalists against one written for everybody who walked in.

Figure 1 — Composition drift. Each step is a sieve, so the surviving population's intent distribution shifts right and narrows. Late-funnel step rates are inflated by this selection, which is why a raw ranking of steps by drop-off systematically indicts the top of the funnel.

The second thing an expert does is separate the steps the user controls from the steps the firm controls. At step 3, Nithaar loses 33,600 people — the largest absolute loss anywhere in the funnel, and larger than the 13,042 that has the growth team agitated. But step 3 is the credit bureau pull and the policy engine. Those 33,600 people were declined. The funnel renders an underwriting decision in exactly the same visual grammar as a slow-loading screen. A team that optimises step 3 is not reducing friction; it is loosening credit policy, which is a different decision, taken by a different officer, under RBI supervision. This is the general principle that the naming of the metric obscures: some drop-off is the product working. A sieve is judged by what it holds back.

The third move is the counterfactual arithmetic, and this is where competent practitioners most often go wrong. The standard projection for improving step k is:

Δ conversions = Nk−1 × Δrk × ∏j>k rj

Applied to Nithaar: if the Account Aggregator flow lifts step 5 from 62 to 78 percent, the incremental survivors are 34,320 × 0.16 = 5,491, and carrying them through the remaining chain 0.73 × 0.85 × 0.95 = 0.5894 gives 3,236 extra disbursals, a 25.8 percent increase in monthly originations. That number is wrong, and it is wrong in a direction that always flatters the proposal. The formula assumes downstream rates are invariant to the change, but the people you newly admit are, by construction, the ones who previously failed — lower-propensity, thin-file, disproportionately self-employed. Their downstream chain is not the average chain.

Figure 2 — The marginal-user correction. Using average downstream rates and average unit economics overstates the value of fixing step 5 by a factor of 2.7. The error is systematic, not random, and it is the single most common quantitative mistake in funnel-driven prioritisation.

Two further mechanics are usually left implicit. The first is the yield arithmetic the industrial tradition brings: a seven-step flow at 95 percent per step converts at 0.957 = 69.8 percent, and deleting one 95 percent step returns 3.7 points, which frequently exceeds what a quarter of design work on the worst step returns. The question "which step leaks most?" has a sibling that is usually more valuable: "which step could not exist?" The second is noise. The standard error of a step rate is √(r(1−r)/n), and n shrinks as you descend. Chhalni's step 6 — paid pilot signed — rested on 34 accounts at 56 percent, giving a standard error of 8.5 points and a 95 percent interval running from roughly 39 to 73 percent. Devang's quarterly deck had been narrating ten-point movements in that step as strategy for a year.

4. When the Model Holds, and When It Lies

Three failures are visible in Malini's column, and together they very nearly account for the 62 without any friction story at all. The channel-mix shift means August's step-4 acceptors were not August-of-last-month's acceptors; affiliate traffic on this product historically converts at step 5 around eleven points below organic, and a twelve-point mix shift moves the aggregate by roughly 1.3 points on its own. The logging defect removes another 4.1 points of apparent conversion — 4.1 percent of the 34,320 who should have been counted, which is about 870 people who did verify and were recorded as lost. Adjusted for instrumentation alone the step rate is closer to 64.6 percent. Neither correction makes the leak disappear, but both change what the leak is worth.

The funnel becomes actively misleading in four situations. First, in discovery and browsing, where not proceeding is a normal outcome and the shape of the journey is a network, not a chain. Second, in habitual use, where the right instrument is a retention curve and a funnel simply mislabels ordinary intermittency as loss. Third, wherever a step is a deliberate filter — credit policy, fraud screening, eligibility, a qualification question — because the metric's sign is inverted there and improving it destroys value. Fourth, wherever a legitimate outcome lies outside the funnel: a Chhalni trial that ends when the prospect decides to buy the enterprise edition through field sales is recorded as a dead trial and is in fact the unit's best possible result.

5. Hard Edge Cases

Five situations break the standard reading, and each has an honest and a dishonest organisational response.

Multi-product. Nithaar's entry event is shared between the loan journey and the savings journey; a single "started" funnel is a mixture of two populations with different intents, and the mixture weight moves with whatever the home screen is currently merchandising. The honest treatment is to declare the product at step 1 and maintain separate funnels; the common treatment is to keep one chart and quietly attribute its movements to whichever product recently shipped something.

Two-sided. Chhanti Bazaar, a Jaipur-based wholesale marketplace matching kirana retailers to regional distributors, watched its buyer-side search-to-order rate fall eight points over a quarter. No buyer-side release explained it. The cause was on the other side: distributor stock-out rates had risen, so searches increasingly returned unavailable SKUs. On a two-sided platform a step rate is a function of the other side's liquidity, and a buyer-funnel leak may be un-fixable by the buyer team. Mature marketplaces read the two funnels jointly and hold a shared metric; less mature ones give each side its own OKR and spend a year optimising against each other.

Regulated. Nithaar's steps 4, 6 and 7 exist because the RBI's digital lending framework requires a Key Fact Statement, verified identity and an explicit mandate, and the DPDP consent screen sits inside step 5. A product manager cannot remove them; the achievable work is entirely in how the mandatory content is presented, sequenced and pre-filled. Reporting drop-off on a regulator-mandated step without labelling it as such produces quarters of misdirected roadmap argument.

Hardware plus software. Pavitra Aqua, a Coimbatore manufacturer of connected reverse-osmosis water purifiers, has a funnel that crosses the boundary of the digital product at the order step: after it come dispatch, a technician visit, and installation, logged by a field-service app with a latency of hours and a completion discipline set by incentives rather than instrumentation. The drop between "ordered" and "installed" is real money, but it is a logistics metric wearing a product metric's clothes, and the team that can move it does not report to the head of product.

AI-native. Chhanak Labs builds an AI assistant that drafts regulatory submissions for medical-device manufacturers. Its funnel has a step — "accepted the first draft" — at which two users can be standing in front of materially different products, because the generation they received differed in quality. Drop-off at that step is a quality distribution, not an interface problem, and it will not respond to design work at all. Worse, the retry loop is indistinguishable from abandonment in a naive funnel: a user who regenerates four times and then accepts looks, in a strict session-scoped funnel, like a user who failed three times. The disciplined treatment is to make the step's quality score a covariate and cut the funnel by it.

At organisational seams the pattern is consistent: the leak sits at the boundary and no one's objective covers it. At Nithaar, steps 1 to 4 belong to growth and steps 5 to 8 to the lending operations group; the 62 percent is precisely the handover. What mature companies say they do is assign an end-to-end owner. What they actually do, in most cases Malini had seen, is hold a monthly reconciliation in which two teams present the same number with different denominators, and the outcome is determined by which of the two the CEO trusts more.

6. Eight Things Experts See That Others Do Not

1. Late steps look good because they face better people. The tell-tale sign of an expert is that they will not compare two step rates without first asking whether the populations are comparable, and will often recut the whole funnel restricted to a single intent-matched segment before drawing any conclusion. The obvious reading — "our e-sign step is excellent, our verification step is terrible" — is wrong because it treats a selection artefact as a design verdict, and it reliably pushes investment toward the top of the funnel where the raw drop-offs are largest and the users are least valuable.

2. The marginal user is not the average user. The tell-tale sign is a practitioner who, when shown a projected lift, immediately asks what downstream rates were assumed for the incremental cohort. The obvious reading applies the funnel's average downstream chain to the newly admitted users; that assumption is not merely optimistic but structurally biased, because the users a fix admits are the ones the old step correctly identified as least likely to finish. In regulated or credit-bearing products the bias compounds, since the marginal cohort is also worse on the economics, as Figure 2 shows.

3. Some drop-off is the sieve working. The tell-tale sign is the question "who do we want to lose here, and are we losing them?" Fraud screens, credit policy, eligibility gates and honest pricing pages all exist to remove people, and their drop-off should be read against a target, not minimised. The obvious reading treats every red bar as a defect; the expensive version of that error is a team that celebrates lifting a qualification step's conversion and discovers the cost two quarters later in charge-offs, churn or support load.

4. A silent logging failure is indistinguishable from abandonment. The tell-tale sign is an analyst who, on seeing a step degrade sharply between releases, checks the app version and the server-side reconciliation before writing a sentence about users. The obvious reading is that behaviour changed; the alternative — that the event stopped firing on one OS version, or that a new SDK batched events past the session boundary — is at least as common, and it is the only explanation that can be ruled in or out in an afternoon. Nithaar's Android defect was found this way, by comparing 4.1 percent of client events against the verification service's own logs.

5. Where you draw step 1 determines every number downstream. The tell-tale sign is that an expert asks what the denominator is before reacting to any percentage. Move Nithaar's entry event from "tapped Check my offer" to "entered PAN" and overall conversion jumps from 10.5 to 13.1 percent with no change whatsoever to the product. This makes cross-company funnel benchmarks nearly worthless and makes internal comparisons across a redesign hazardous, because redesigns frequently move the entry event without anyone noticing that they have.

6. Deleting a step usually beats improving one. The tell-tale sign is a practitioner who counts steps before measuring them. The obvious reading looks for the worst rate; the yield arithmetic says that a chain's output is the product of its terms, so a step at 90 percent that could be merged into its neighbour returns more than a heroic effort to move a 60 percent step to 66. Chhalni's mandate and agreement steps at Nithaar's equivalent — separate screens for e-NACH and e-signature, at 85 and 95 percent — were combinable into one at roughly 90, worth about 1.5 points of overall conversion for two weeks of work.

7. Time-to-step carries as much information as pass-rate. Two steps with identical 70 percent conversion, one resolving in eight seconds and one in eight days, are different products with different failure mechanisms and different fixes. The tell-tale sign is an expert who asks for the distribution of elapsed time at the step, not just the rate, and who notices bimodality — a fast mode and a slow mode usually means two populations, such as Chhalni's self-serve teams who connect a data source in an afternoon and its regulated pharma accounts who cannot until security review completes.

8. The aggregate funnel is a mixture, and mixtures reverse. Simpson's paradox is not exotic in funnels; it is routine, because acquisition mix moves faster than product quality. The tell-tale sign is an expert who checks whether every segment moved in the direction the aggregate moved before accepting the aggregate's story. A redesign can raise the step rate for iOS and for Android separately while lowering the blended rate, if the release coincided with a campaign that shifted volume toward the weaker platform — and the team will spend a month rolling back an improvement.

7. What Actually Differs Across Product Types

The differences are real in three places and overstated everywhere else. Cadence and sample size genuinely differ: Nithaar can read a one-point move in a step rate as money because 120,000 entrants make the standard error about 0.14 points, while Chhalni's 340 trials make anything short of a twenty-point move indistinguishable from noise, so B2B funnels must be read as slow cohort curves and never as daily dashboards. The unit of analysis genuinely differs: in enterprise and platform contexts the converting entity is an account containing several humans with distinct roles, and a user-grain funnel will show a "drop-off" at the step where the champion hands over to procurement, which is progress, not loss. Observability genuinely differs: in hardware and physical-goods journeys, and in any journey with a human in the loop, the decisive steps happen where the product cannot see, and the funnel silently ends at the last instrumented event.

What does not meaningfully differ is the analytical discipline. The selection argument in Figure 1, the marginal-user correction in Figure 2, the censoring problem, the mixture problem and the instrumentation problem apply identically to a consumer app, an enterprise trial, a marketplace and an AI assistant. Claims that B2B funnels "work differently" usually turn out to be claims about sample size and time constants, which are quantitative differences, not conceptual ones.

Stage changes the correct posture more than product type does. A pre-fit company with a few thousand entrants should treat its funnel as a hypothesis-generator and spend its effort on the qualitative layer, because at that volume nearly every movement is noise and the biggest risk is a wrong product rather than a leaky one. A company at Nithaar's scale should treat the funnel as an accounting system with a standing owner, a change log for event definitions, and an experiment attached to every proposed step change. A late-stage company's distinctive problem is neither: it is that the funnel has been forked into eleven variants across five teams, and the argument in the room is no longer about users at all.

8. Three Worked Cases

Chhalni Systems: the leak that was a clock

Sujata Menon's challenge was testable. Her team re-ran the Q2 cohort with a 180-day maturity window instead of 90 days and plotted cumulative step-3 conversion against elapsed days since trial start.

Figure 3 — Right-censoring in a B2B funnel. Of the 181 workspaces recorded as lost at step 3 under a 90-day window, 47 connected between days 91 and 150. More than a quarter of the apparent leak was the reporting clock, not the product.

Step 3 conversion rose from 29 percent (74 of 255) to 47.5 percent (121 of 255) purely by extending the window. The residual leak was still large, but its composition had changed: among the 134 that never connected even at 180 days, 61 had opened a security questionnaire and never returned it, and 38 had never invited a technical user at all. Devang did not fund the connector rebuild. He funded two smaller things — a pre-filled security questionnaire pack triggered at workspace creation, and a prompt to invite an IT contact in the first session — and changed the unit's reporting to a 150-day cohort curve. Two quarters later, step 3 at 150 days stood at 58 percent on a cohort of 391.

Pavitra Aqua: the fix that worked and lost money

Pavitra Aqua's direct-to-consumer flow included a "check your water" step: pincode plus an optional TDS reading, producing a model recommendation. It was easily the leakiest step in the funnel — of 23,200 monthly starts, only 10,208 finished — and in March 2026 the growth team removed it, defaulting every visitor to the mid-range model. Malini's team decomposed the 13,042 lost at step 5 rather than treating it as one population. Three thousand nine hundred and ten had abandoned within eleven seconds of the screen loading, before any upload could plausibly have been attempted — a price-and-terms reaction arriving late, not a friction event. Eight hundred and seventy were the Android logging defect. Two thousand two hundred and sixty had started an upload and failed it, with a heavy concentration in files above 8 MB and in statements from two co-operative banks whose PDF format the parser rejected. The remaining 6,002 had opened the screen, spent over a minute, and left — the genuine friction cohort, and the only one an Account Aggregator flow would address. Sizing the fix against 6,002 rather than 13,042, and applying marginal rather than average downstream rates, produced an expected gain of roughly ₹19 lakh a month against an engineering cost of eleven weeks — still positive, but no longer the quarter's obvious priority.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Does the funnel rank opportunities at all? The experimentalist position, in its strongest form, is that drop-off is an observational quantity generated by a process in which the step both blocks and sorts, so the ordering of steps by loss carries no reliable information about the ordering of steps by the value of intervening. The evidence is a long record of shipped step-level improvements that failed to move terminal conversion — Pavitra's case, plus the well-documented tendency of onboarding wins to evaporate in aggregate. The opposing position holds that experiments are expensive, slow and impossible below a certain volume, and that a funnel plus a marginal-user correction plus a segment cut is a good enough prior to choose between candidates. For the experimentalists to be wrong, it would have to be shown that observational step rankings correlate reasonably with experimentally measured lift across a body of cases; nobody has published such a body, largely because firms do not run the experiments they would need to build it.

Sessions or users, strict or loose? The session-scoped, strict-order camp argues that the funnel should model the product as designed, because that is the thing the team can change; a user who returns tomorrow and completes is a different attempt and should be counted as one. The user-scoped, loose-order camp argues that the firm is paid by people, not attempts, and that a session-scoped funnel manufactures drop-off out of ordinary human behaviour — a person who compares two lenders over three evenings is not leaking. Both are internally consistent; they optimise different things. The disagreement becomes empirical only when you can measure what share of session-level "drop-offs" convert within thirty days, and firms that measure it are frequently surprised: at Nithaar the figure was 11 percent, which is small; in higher-consideration categories it can exceed a third, at which point the session-scoped funnel is simply the wrong instrument.

Benchmarks or self-comparison? The benchmarking camp holds that a checkout converting at 31 percent when comparable Indian marketplaces convert at 45 should be investigated regardless of internal trend, and that refusing external reference points lets teams normalise mediocrity. The self-comparison camp holds, following nuance 5 above, that a funnel's numbers are functions of where its author chose to place step 1 and how the events were defined, so cross-company comparison is measuring definitional choices with a rounding error of behaviour on top. The steelman for benchmarks is that the definitional noise, while large, is not correlated with performance, so a big gap is still informative; the steelman against is that the definitional variance is frequently larger than the performance variance being detected. What would settle it is a standardised event schema adopted across firms, which the industry has repeatedly attempted and never sustained.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied drop-off can build the chart, name the worst step and write a plausible sentence about why users leave. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask about the denominator and the window before they react to any percentage, every time, including when the number is good. They decompose a loss before sizing a fix, because they have learned that a single step almost always contains three or four populations with different causes and that the fix addresses one of them. They hold two ledgers for every step — what it costs and what it filters — and they are willing to argue for making a step harder. And they treat the funnel as an instrument that produces questions of a specific shape, then go and get the answer somewhere else: session recordings, five support tickets read end to end, a call with two customers who abandoned. The behavioural signature is a reluctance to write a causal sentence and an eagerness to write a decomposition.

12. The Decisions

On 22 September, Malini presented to Nithaar's board a single slide: the 13,042 broken into four populations, the instrumentation correction applied, and the Account Aggregator proposal sized against 6,002 users at marginal rather than average downstream rates — ₹19 lakh a month, eleven weeks. She recommended shipping the two cheap fixes first (the PDF parser for the two co-operative banks, worth an estimated 1,100 users a month at negligible cost, and the Android logging repair) and deferring the Account Aggregator build by a quarter. Farhan Qureshi's step 3 was left alone and relabelled on every dashboard as "policy decision," not drop-off. The reasoning she gave the board was that the number she had been sent to fix was four numbers wearing one coat, and that only one of them was a product problem.

Devang Puri, on 9 September, declined to fund the connector rebuild, moved his unit's reporting to a 150-day cohort curve, and shipped the security-questionnaire pack and the invite-an-IT-contact prompt. His argument to his CEO was uncomfortable and he made it anyway: the number on which the unit's strategy had rested for a year had been substantially an artefact of a reporting window chosen because the quarter is ninety days long.

Three questions for discussion. First: Malini relabelled step 3 as a policy decision rather than a leak. Who in an organisation should have the authority to make that reclassification, and what stops it from becoming a way to make inconvenient losses disappear? Second: Devang's 150-day window makes his unit's funnel honest and also makes it useless for quarterly management. What should he report to a board that meets four times a year? Third: Pavitra Aqua's growth team followed the funnel correctly, shipped the change the data indicated, and destroyed value. What would a review process have to look like for that decision to have been caught before launch rather than four months after it?

Sadhan Gold: The Step Before Dhanteras

Aparna Iyer has one engineering team, six weeks, and a funnel with three plausible leaks. Dhanteras does not move.

1. Seventeen days to code freeze

On the evening of Tuesday, 22 September 2026, Aparna Iyer stayed back in Sadhan Gold's office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru after the rest of the product floor had emptied. On her screen was a single slide she would present to the executive committee on Friday, and on the whiteboard behind her was the only fact that really mattered: code freeze for the festive release was 24 October, and Dhanteras fell on 6 November. Gold-buying in India is seasonal in a way few products are. Roughly a third of Sadhan's annual purchase volume would pass through the three weeks around Dhanteras and Diwali, and whatever the team shipped by 24 October was what customers would meet during that window.

Devika Krishnan, Sadhan's chief executive, had given Aparna a target rather than a plan: 25,000 active Gold SIP subscribers by 31 December, against 11,400 at the end of August. Aparna had one squad of nine engineers and one design resource. She had to pick a step in the funnel and commit to it by Friday.

2. Sadhan Gold

Sadhan Gold, founded in Hyderabad in 2021 and headquartered in Bengaluru since 2023, sold 24-karat digital gold to retail savers. A customer could buy from ₹100 upwards; the metal was held in insured vaults by a refiner-partner and could be redeemed as coins delivered to the customer's address or sold back at the live rate. Sadhan earned a spread on each purchase and a small custody fee. The product that mattered commercially was not the one-time purchase but the Gold SIP: a standing instruction, executed through a UPI Autopay mandate registered with the customer's bank under NPCI's framework, that bought a fixed rupee amount of gold every week or every month.

The market around Sadhan was crowded and largely owned by companies far bigger than it. Digital gold was already available inside PhonePe, Paytm and Groww; the metal itself was supplied by refiners such as MMTC-PAMP and Augmont; Tanishq's long-running jewellery savings schemes remained the default for a great many Indian families; and gold ETFs on Zerodha and other broking platforms served the more financially literate saver. Sadhan's argument for existing was narrow and, so far, defensible: it was the only one of these that treated small, habitual gold saving as the whole product rather than as a tab inside something else. Its average SIP was ₹850 a month, and its typical customer was between 24 and 38, in a tier-2 city, with a household that had bought gold at weddings and festivals for three generations.

By August 2026, Sadhan had 6.4 lakh registered customers, 11,400 active SIPs, and monthly purchase volume of ₹41 crore. It had raised ₹210 crore across two rounds. The unit economics were unambiguous about which customer mattered.

3. The situation

In July, Nikhil Menon, Sadhan's data scientist in Toronto, had rebuilt the acquisition funnel properly for the first time — consistent denominators, a 30-day window, first-time users only, strict step order. The result, Exhibit 1, was circulated on a Friday and had been argued about ever since.

The step with the worst conversion in the funnel was mandate registration: of the customers who began setting up a Gold SIP, only 40.4 percent ended with a live mandate. That number had been stable for eleven months. It was the number Rohit Sathe's engineers in Pune complained about, the number that generated the most customer-support tickets per thousand users who touched it, and the number Aparna had privately assumed she would be fixing this quarter.

Nikhil's memo made an inconvenient observation. Measured in people rather than percentages, the mandate step lost 8,700 customers in August. The PAN and KYC step lost 80,000. Even allowing for the fact that a customer who has begun a SIP setup is far more valuable than one who has just signed up, the two steps were closer in rupee terms than anyone on the team had assumed, and a third step — the gap between a completed KYC and a first purchase — lost 51,000.

Three people in three time zones read the same exhibit and drew different conclusions, which is the position Aparna found herself arbitrating.

Rohit Sathe, engineering lead in Pune, had pulled the payment-service-provider logs for the mandate step and produced Exhibit 2. His reading was that most of the loss was mechanical and fixable: long bank redirect chains, OTP pages that timed out, and a callback that Sadhan's app sometimes failed to receive, leaving customers who had actually authorised a mandate looking at an error screen. He estimated six weeks of work for a rebuild with a net-banking e-mandate fallback, which meant it would land after code freeze, in mid-November.

Lena Brandt, the designer, worked from Berlin and had spent two weeks watching session recordings in the overlap hours of her morning and India's afternoon. Her conclusion was that the mandate step was not primarily a technical failure but a comprehension failure. Customers who had cheerfully bought ₹500 of gold moments earlier stopped at a screen that asked them to authorise a recurring debit of up to ₹15,000 — the mandate cap, set high so that a customer could increase their SIP later without re-registering. In eleven of the thirty-one recordings she reviewed, the customer reached the bank's authorisation page, scrolled to the amount, and closed the app.

Sharanya Rao, the customer-success lead in Singapore, covered Sadhan's small but fast-growing non-resident segment, much of it in Dubai, where Indian families buying gold was hardly a novelty. Her queue told a different story about a different step. Non-resident customers were failing at PAN and KYC, not at the mandate: they either lacked a PAN linked to an Indian mobile number or could not complete the address check. The segment was 4 percent of installs and, among those who did get through, carried an average SIP of ₹3,100 — almost four times the domestic average. Sharanya had 190 open tickets from Gulf customers and a partnership conversation, opened by Vikram Nair from New Jersey, with a remittance firm that wanted to bundle Sadhan into its Gulf-to-India product before the festive season.

6. The options

Option A: rebuild mandate registration. Six weeks, the full squad, landing around 12 November — after Dhanteras. It addresses the worst percentage in the funnel and the loudest internal complaint, would recover the 790 misinformed customers immediately, and permanently reduces a tax the team pays every quarter. Its cost is that it misses the festive window entirely, and, on Exhibit 2's own evidence, it cannot touch the 38.6 percent of failures that are abandonment rather than mechanics.

Option B: reframe the mandate step before freeze. Two weeks: lower the default mandate cap from ₹15,000 to three times the chosen SIP amount, explain the debit in rupees on Sadhan's own screen before handing the customer to the bank, and add a reconciliation job that catches the 790. Ships on 6 October, in time for Dhanteras. Its cost is that it is a bet on Lena's reading of thirty-one recordings, it leaves the bank-side failures untouched, and a lower cap means customers must re-register to increase their SIP later — a future drop-off in exchange for a present one.

Option C: move up the funnel. Spend the quarter on step 4 — the ₹96 lakh gap between KYC and first purchase — and on non-resident KYC, which Sharanya and Vikram need before the remittance partnership. This is the largest pool of lost value in Exhibit 1 and the only option that serves the highest-value segment. Its cost is that step 4 is the least understood step in the funnel: nobody yet knows whether those 46,400 customers are confused, uninterested, or merely waiting for a gold price they consider fair. Committing a festive quarter to a step no one has diagnosed is a considerable act of faith.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1 alone, rank the six steps by the size of the opportunity they represent. What does your ranking assume, and where would the ranking change if the assumption were wrong?

2. Exhibit 2 splits mandate failures into six outcomes. Which of these are product problems, which are partner problems, and which are neither? What would you do about the 1,140 attempts with no recorded outcome before drawing any conclusion?

3. Lena's evidence is thirty-one session recordings; Nikhil's is 3.1 lakh users. In what way is each of them better evidence than the other, and what would you ask for that neither has produced?

4. It is Friday morning. What do you tell Devika, and what do you commit the squad to for the seventeen days before code freeze? What do you deliberately choose not to do, and how will you know in December whether you chose correctly?

8. A note for the learner

This case is an exercise in reading drop-off, and the lens does three things here.

First, it converts percentages into people and people into rupees. The mandate step's 40.4 percent is the most alarming number in Exhibit 1 and the fifth-largest opportunity in it. The habit the case is trying to build is the reflex to multiply: users lost at a step, times the probability they would have converted, times what a conversion is worth. Do that and the funnel reorders itself. Aparna's instinct to fix the worst percentage was the instinct of a competent manager reading a chart naively.

Second, it insists that a funnel says where and never why. Exhibit 2 is unusual in that someone went and found out. Once the mandate step is decomposed, the single number 40.4 percent turns out to contain at least three different problems with three different owners, of which the engineering rebuild addresses the smallest. Most funnels in most companies have never been decomposed this way, and the discipline the case rewards is asking for the decomposition before authorising the work.

Third, it shows what segmentation does to an average. Exhibit 3's non-resident customers fail at a completely different step from the domestic majority and are worth several times more each. An aggregate funnel makes such a segment invisible by construction.

One defensible path. Take Option B now and Option C next, and say so explicitly on Friday. The reasoning: the festive window is a genuine constraint and only B fits inside it; B is cheap enough that being wrong costs two weeks rather than a quarter; and the reconciliation fix inside B is unambiguously correct regardless of whose theory of the mandate step is right, since 790 customers are currently being told a mandate failed when it did not. At the same time, commission a two-week diagnostic on step 4 — segmentation by city tier, handset and gold price on the day, twenty user interviews, and a check on whether "no purchase in 30 days" is really abandonment or merely a customer waiting for the rate to fall — so that the January quarter begins with a diagnosed step rather than another argument. Option A is not abandoned; it is deferred until Exhibit 2's abandonment rows have been addressed, because rebuilding a step that 38.6 percent of customers leave before they reach it is engineering applied to the wrong half of the problem.

A learner who instead argues for A or C can still be right, but only by confronting what Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 say. The weak answer is the one that picks the worst percentage and stops.
